articles.text: New Delhi: How long will a peda stay fresh? For India's mithai makers, the question is becoming a business concern ahead of Diwali as tighter food safety rules in several states require the display of manufacturing and use-by dates even on loose sweets.Watchdog agencies in states such as Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand are among those that have made this mandatory. The directive aims to help consumers assess freshness as inspections have revealed that buyers were not always given clear information about when sweets were made or how long they remained suitable for consumption, the agencies said.Also Read: FSSAI issues notice to Zepto over alleged delivery of expired besanHowever, small and medium-sized manufacturers and sellers said that the frequent inspections and notices have made it difficult for them to operate during the festive season, when sales are at their highest. "Determining shelf life for different varieties could mean hiring external agencies, adding to costs and workload during the industry's busiest season," said Firoz H Naqvi, president of the Federation of Sweets and Namkeen Manufacturers.135076403Eye on AdulterationProducts on shelves are replenished many times a day during the busy season, said Naqvi.The Uttar Pradesh Mithai Namkeen Bakery Association recently urged the state food safety department to adopt a what it described as a supportive approach during the festive season, allowing small and medium-sized traditional businesses adequate time, training and technical guidance to formalise such practices.Also Read: Nepal bans import, sales of Indian biscuit Priyagold over food safety violations"For minor documentation, display, record-keeping or other correctable deficiencies, businesses may kindly be guided and given a reasonable opportunity to rectify them, instead of facing immediate disruption of production or disproportionate action," the grouping wrote to the Uttar Pradesh Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) on October 11.Other states such as Maharashtra, Karnataka and Haryana have also stepped up vigilance against adulteration during festivals and other large gatherings, when demand for sweets, edible oils, dairy products and other food items typically rises.Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner Tukaram Mundhe has been on a food safety, hygiene and anti-adulteration crusade that has led to widespread action with inspections of restaurants, hotels, cloud kitchens, dairies, quick-commerce dark stores and manufacturing units.The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has asked states to increase surveillance to prevent the sale of adulterated and counterfeit food items during the festive season. It has also intensified scrutiny of packaged food products, issuing notices to major companies over alleged misleading health and nutritional claims, labelling discrepancies and non-compliance with food regulations.This comes as prices of key ingredients - milk and other dairy products, dry fruits, sugar, gram flour (besan) - have risen to records this year.Impact on marginsThe rising prices of inputs including fuel has had a cascading effect on the end product and will squeeze manufacturers' margins, said Suresh Goel, chief executive officer, Bikanervala Foods."Inspections happen during all festival seasons and so good and hygienic practices have become a part of our processing and packaging systems," he said. Since the Covid pandemic, the industry has aligned itself with health trends with even unorganised players making efforts to adopt best practices, he said.

articles.title: Retired KC-10 Extender Tanker Has Risen From Boneyard To Fly Again
articles.text:
One of the KC-10A Extender aerial refueling tankers the U.S. Air Force retired some two years ago has left the boneyard at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona. This aircraft is one of a set of KC-10As sold to private aerial refueling contractor Omega Air. At least one other potential operator, a still mysterious end user somewhere in North Africa, could also be in line to pick up several ex-Air Force Extenders.

Maxim Loshak, who goes by the handle @az_aviator on X and Instagram, caught the KC-10A leaving Davis-Monthan earlier today. The aircraft currently carries U.S. civil registration number N82247, and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) records confirm that Omega Air is the new owner. Online flight tracking data also shows the aircraft subsequently flew to San Antonio International Airport, which is Omega’s main base of operations.

The KC-10A in question previously carried the Air Force registration number 86-0034 and had been in the boneyard since May 12, 2023, per the service’s records. The Air Force acquired a total of 60 Extender tankers between 1979 and 1987, and lost one in an accident in 1987. The very last of the remaining 59 KC-10As was retired in September 2024. The Extender was derived from the three-engine DC-10 airliner and was designed to refuel aircraft using either the boom or the probe-and-drogue method.

As seen in the picture at the top of this story, N82247 notably lacks the KC-10A’s trademark boom under the rear fuselage. This is actually not entirely unexpected. The Air Force had put 10 Extenders up for auction last year in a non-flyable state. Each of the planes was missing a single engine, taken from under one of their wings, for reasons that are still not entirely clear. These particular aircraft were also among the first KC-10As to be retired, and their booms had been stripped to be used as spares for other examples that had remained in service until the type’s final retirement in 2024.

In addition to sourcing the requisite engines, “in order to make them flyable, the winning bidder will need to work with Boeing to obtain a fly-away kit to seal up the area where the boom systems was,” an Air Force spokesperson told us last year while the 10 KC-10As were still up for auction.

Omega Air could fit new booms to this KC-10A, as well as other ex-USAF Extenders it is in the process of acquiring. The company could also leave some of them configured as probe-and-drogue-only tankers. Omega already flies two ex-Dutch KDC-10 tankers, which are broadly similar to the KC-10, as well as another DC-10 converted into a probe-and-drogue-only tanker. The company has several Boeing 707-based tankers, as well.

There is a possibility that some of the KC-10As that Omega is acquiring could be operated in non-tanker roles. Carrying cargo was also a major role for Extender while in Air Force service. Still, this seems unlikely given that aerial refueling is Omega’s primary business. Some of the ex-Air Force Extenders might also be used as sources of spare parts. TWZ has reached out for more information about Omega’s overall plans for its new acquisitions.

Regardless, even in a boomless configuration, ex-USAF KC-10As will be a significant addition to Omega Air’s fleet. Demand for private aerial refueling services, in general, has been ramping up in the United States and elsewhere globally in recent years.

For the U.S. military, private contractors offer a valuable way to reduce demand for and strain on organic tanker fleets to meet non-combat-related aerial refueling needs. This, in turn, helps free up government-owned tankers for combat missions and other higher-priority taskings. Those tankers may also simply not need to fly as much with private companies helping to shift the burden. The ability of the Air Force’s existing tanker fleets, in particular, to meet even peacetime demands has been a growing point of concern for years now. This has been further exacerbated by persistent technical and other issues with replacement KC-46 tankers.

With all this in mind, the Air Force’s decision to retire the KC-10A fleet entirely was and still is controversial. Though the Extenders were certainly aging, they were also highly flexible tankers able to carry greater loads of fuel than the KC-46s that supplanted them.

Omega Air clearly still sees value in the KC-10A. As mentioned, at least one other operator in North Africa is at least interested in potentially acquiring Extenders. Others may yet emerge.

If nothing else, after just over two years, an ex-USAF KC-10A has returned to the skies for a second career in the private sector.

Special thanks again to Maxim Loshak for sharing his picture of N82247 with us.

articles.title: Cops raid office of RFK Jr. allies planning “unethical” vaccine trial on babies
articles.text:
Police in Guinea-Bissau raided the offices of Danish researchers on Monday, seizing doses of hepatitis B vaccine intended for a vaccine trial for newborns. International health experts have called the trial "unethical," but anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has attempted to fund it with US taxpayer dollars.

Under Kennedy, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced in December that it had awarded the Danish researchers—led by married couple Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project—an unsolicited $1.6 million grant to run the trial. Aaby and Stabell Benn are controversial vaccine researchers who claim vaccines cause overlooked harms. They have been repeatedly praised by Kennedy, but are currently under investigation for alleged scientific misconduct by Danish authorities.

Plans for the trial were halted in January as widespread condemnation erupted over the trial's design, which would potentially expose thousands of newborns in the country to hepatitis B, risking a lifelong infection that can lead to liver cirrhosis, cancer, and premature death. Outrage flared again after a Rolling Stone story earlier this month claimed the CDC set aside another $1.6 million in funding in late September and planned to move forward with the trial.

articles.title: Microsoft reportedly projects $1,200 to $1,800 price for 2028 Project Helix
articles.text:
We haven't heard many details about Microsoft's upcoming "Project Helix" gaming hardware since the company announced it in March as a device that will "play your Xbox and PC games." articles.title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
articles.text:
Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise. 

The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down.

In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying. 

The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all.

The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access.

“Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.” 

The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science.

“One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”

articles.title: Here’s the tea
articles.text:
When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773. 

But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later. The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done. He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s.

Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store. Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s.

The discovery does not make the label historically insignificant, he says. Instead, what began as an inquiry into a supposed artifact of the Boston Tea Party became a study of how ordinary objects acquire historical authority, and how historical memory itself is made.

“History is never finished,” he says. “Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions.”

articles.title: Melt it, spin it, use it again
articles.text:
The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn. 

The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon. Those fibers would have to be separated for recycling—a process that isn’t practical. But the MIT team found a way to create a similarly stretchy yarn from two variations of polyethylene, a material commonly used in milk jugs and grocery bags. Because they come from the same chemical family, the yarn can be melted as is. Svetlana Boriskina, who led the work as a research scientist in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, says a garment made from this material could then be spun into new yarn for a next generation of clothing. Even after 10 cycles of melting and respinning, the yarn stays as strong and flexible as conventional thread. 

“Now we have something that can be knitted and woven,” Boriskina says. “That is the next stage.” Someday, the researchers hope, a polyethylene garment could be dropped in a collection bin and sent to a recycling facility, promoting a more sustainable, circular textile economy.

articles.title: A reason to eat carbs
articles.text:
A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help some people lose weight, and some research has shown that it may protect against colon cancer. But a new study suggests that such a ketogenic diet may also increase the risk of cancer in the small intestine.

This type of diet forces the body to burn fatty acids instead of carbohydrates for fuel, producing by-products called ketone bodies. One of these, BHB, was thought to be responsible for the protective effect observed against colon cancer.

Omer Yilmaz, director of the MIT Stem Cell Initiative, worked with colleagues including MIT postdocs Jessica Shay and Fangtao Chi to investigate whether the effects were similar in the small intestine. But instead, they found that mice on a ketogenic diet were more likely to develop tumors in that part of the gastrointestinal system than those on a control diet were. 

Additional studies revealed that this tumor growth was driven by the way intestinal cells burn dietary fat for energy—a metabolic pathway called fatty acid oxidation. This pathway activates proteins that signal stem cells to multiply more rapidly. 

“Having more stem cells means that when you injure the small intestine, it can repair itself better, but the downside is that having more active stem cells can lead to tumor formation,” Yilmaz says.

Though the researchers confirmed that a ketogenic diet suppressed the development of colon tumors, their findings suggest that ketone bodies are not involved. “These molecules are essentially metabolic bystanders,” Yilmaz says.

One implication is that commercial ketone supplements probably do little to either help or harm people who take them. But the deeper issue is “why the same diet has opposite consequences in two adjacent parts of the gut,” Chi says. “That is what we are working to understand next.”

Whatever they discover, as Yilmaz says, “the message here is that we need to be very careful in generalizing the effects that these diets can have.”

Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. articles.title: Tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs sit idle in Meta's Prometheus supercluster, just waiting for a failure
articles.text:
More than 11 percent of the GPUs at Meta’s Prometheus supercluster in New Albany, Ohio, are either dead or sitting idle waiting to step in when the next drops out, Zuckercorp revealed this week.

The massive pool of redundant GPUs is just one of several measures the hyperscaler has taken to keep its AI training runs on track.

Prometheus is among Meta's largest compute deployments to date. Powered by Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and (soon) Vera Rubin rack systems, Meta says the supercluster will eventually scale to a gigawatt of capacity spanning about a million accelerators.

But as anyone who has worked on a large scale compute cluster understands, whether for LLM training or traditional HPC workloads, more chips inevitably means more problems.

In an eight-GPU node, the chance of having a GPU fail is relatively low. In a 100,000-GPU cluster, failures are unavoidable. Meta is building something that's 10x larger and requires distributed training runs across multiple datacenters. Keeping the entire thing humming long enough to reach the next checkpoint becomes a major headache.

In a blog post published this week, Meta offered a unique look at the work it's done to keep failures from derailing the development of models like Muse Spark or its most recent release Muse Wonder.

Idle GPUs are the cost of continuity

When Meta began the first phase of its Prometheus deployment in New Albany, the company says, it was experiencing roughly 1,000 interruptions per day for every 8,000 GPUs.

Interruptions don't mean GPU failure. They simply mean something crashed, failed, or timed out, forcing the training run to stop and roll back to the last known good checkpoint.

Meta claims in the year since it's been able to cut down the number of interruptions by 99 percent, to about 11 per day per 8,000 GPUs.

One of the ways it's done this is by keeping some of Prometheus' GPUs in reserve. The cluster is currently powered by a combination of GB200 and GB300 systems, each with 72 GPUs per NVLink domain. However, only 64 of them are ever in use at any given moment. The other eight are essentially hot spares.

Meta did this because a single failed GPU would take out an entire rack and interrupt the training run. Now, when a GPU fails, one of the spares can slot in and take its place. While this saves time — Meta doesn't have to drop the entire rack from the cluster or wait for someone to swap the faulty component to start training again — a failed GPU would still result in an interruption, albeit a shorter one.

Parallel resiliency

To mitigate this, Meta took advantage of the fact that large scale training jobs usually use data parallelism, where multiple copies of the model are resident within the cluster.

"When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training," Meta explained. "The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput."

In other words, Meta's training runs only get interrupted if the fault exceeds the data parallel domain. When this happens, the company has implemented a comprehensive checkpointing scheme, which you can think of a bit like auto-save or a revision history. That way if something does fail, Meta doesn't have to start over from scratch.

"Our distributed checkpointing architecture asynchronously saves the model state — including gradients and optimizer data — to multi-tier storage," the company wrote.

NVLink growing pains

Meta says one of the most difficult challenges was making the NVLink fabrics used to connect 72 GPUs behave like one great big accelerator. Earlier H100 and H200-based systems featured just eight GPUs per NVLink domain, which meant the links were far shorter and less numerous. But this functionality was expanded nine-fold with Nvidia's Blackwell generation.

"With over 600,000 NVLink connections, even marginal signal degradation triggers frequent NVLink recovery cycles," the company wrote.

To overcome this, Meta had to implement a continuous telemetry system and conduct L11 diagnostic burns to isolate weak links before the systems were put into production.

Power was another challenge. Ramping up and down tens of thousands of GPUs for a training run can introduce massive spikes in power consumption called transients, which can overwhelm power supply equipment.

According to Meta, by focusing on the stability and reliability of its cluster, it was able to achieve more than 85 percent "goodput" — a measure of useful throughput — for pretraining and more than 90 percent for reinforcement learning on its latest model Muse Wonder.

The company's ambitions don't stop here. As it works its way toward a million GPUs, Meta hopes to get its interruption rate down to just two per day for every 8,000 GPUs, or about 100,000 GPU-hours mean time between interrupts. ®

articles.title: OpenBSD 8.0 arrives with security record still intact
articles.text:
OpenBSD 8.0 is here, marking the project's 61st release and continuing its schedule of semiannual releases dating back to 1996. What started more than 30 years ago as a fork of NetBSD has grown into one of the most security-conscious operating systems in active development. In a post to the project's announcements mailing list, OpenBSD founder Theo de Raadt highlights a host of improvements included with the latest version and writes that the project remains "proud of OpenBSD's record of more than thirty years with only two remote holes in the default install."

The latest OpenBSD version brings new features and improvements across the board. These changes, particularly the new Intel Arc support and expanded virtual address space, should improve compatibility with modern graphics cards and allow the system to map more than 4GB of VRAM. Some of the major updates noted in the release newsletter are as follows:

  • Added support for Intel Arc A-Series (DG2/Alchemist) graphics cards.
  • 512GB kernel virtual address space on AMD64, up from 4GB, allowing VRAM mapping above 4GB.
  • Added hibernation support for ARM64 systems.
  • A new RPKI-to-router daemon: rtrd(8).
  • RISC-V improvements including kernel support for the 'V' vector extension and support for Advanced Interrupt Architecture.
  • Wireless network driver additions and improvements, including 802.11n and 40 MHz channels for the qwx(4) wireless driver.
  • Added support for up to 64 virtual CPUs per guest virtual machine.
  • Security and internal improvements for LibreSSL 4.4.0 and OpenSSH 10.6.
  • Improvements to the vmm/vmd virtualization stack.

The new OpenBSD also retires support for Loongson architecture after the port stopped working with the Clang 22 compiler. If you're interested in reading over all the changes that come with the new OpenBSD 8.0, you can take a look at the release announcement.

articles.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
articles.text:
Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet.

As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices.

One word: bonkers

The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here - Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide.

articles.title: Quantum error correction goes well beyond breakeven
articles.text:
Running complicated algorithms on quantum computing hardware is going to require the use of logical qubits, where collections of hardware qubits are linked together in ways that allow errors to be detected and corrected. In general, the more hardware qubits you dedicate to each logical qubit, the better the chances are of identifying errors. But, given that the hardware qubits are prone to errors, adding more of them also increases the probability that errors will occur. If the hardware error rate is too high, then growing the logical qubit will only make matters worse.

Fortunately, several companies have demonstrated hardware where the error rate is not too high. Several demonstrations show logical qubits are beyond the breakeven point, where adding more qubits improves performance. The problem is that the improvement isn't very dramatic. To lower error rates to levels we'll need to run complex algorithms, we'd have to add a completely impractical number of qubits to each logical qubit.

On Monday, Quantinuum announced that its current generation of hardware is capable of scaling well beyond the breakeven point. Each step up in the size of logical qubits improved some measures of their performance by a factor of over 10.

articles.title: Palo Alto's firewall OS has been under attack from multiple ransomware groups since June
articles.text:
Multiple ransomware groups, including Qilin and Inc, have been exploiting a high-severity authentication bypass bug in Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS, with Unit 42 investigating attacks since early June across numerous industries, such as finance, healthcare, and manufacturing.

CVE-2026-0257 affects PAN-OS GlobalProtect portals and gateways, potentially allowing attackers to bypass security restrictions and establish an unauthorized VPN connection.

The security vendor first disclosed and patched the bug on May 13 and initially assigned it a medium-severity rating, saying it was aware of attempts to exploit it but had not observed any malicious exploitation.

That assessment quickly changed, and by the end of the month, Rapid7 researchers said they observed successful exploitation across multiple customer environments dating back to at least May 17.

On Monday, Palo Alto Networks’ consulting and incident response biz, Unit 42, said ransomware crews including Qilin and Inc continue to batter the CVE.

“Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session,” said Andy Piazza, a senior director of threat intelligence at Unit 42.

After gaining initial access, the criminals move laterally across the networks using Remote Desktop Protocol and Server Message Block (SMB), dropping additional malware for credential harvesting and data theft before ultimately deploying ransomware, Piazza warned.

In its ongoing investigations, Unit 42 has spotted the ransomware criminals infecting “numerous industries, including education, financial services, healthcare, high tech, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and wholesale and retail."

Palo Alto Networks did not respond to The Register’s inquiries about the attacks, including how many organizations have been infected.

Additionally, ReliaQuest intel analysts warned that “multiple threat groups,” including Settra ransomware operators, are also exploiting the bug to gain initial access to corporate networks via unauthorized VPN sessions.

“The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer,” Piazza wrote. “In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).”

This allows the miscreants to bypass in-guest endpoint detection and response products, and represents “a highly sophisticated method” of stealing domain-wide credentials, he added.

Unit 42 has also spotted criminals chaining this exploit for initial access with other vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-27532, which targets Veeam backup infrastructure.

So if you haven’t already patched vulnerable PAN-OS software, do so now - and investigate whether attackers have already gained access to your network. Check Unit 42’s indicators of compromise to assist with threat-hunting activities.®

articles.title: Swamped curl maintainers take low-level flaws public to survive vulnerability 'avalanche'
articles.text:
An "avalanche of vulnerability reports" is forcing curl to move lower-severity cases into public view, reserving private handling for high and critical flaws.

From October 26, low and medium-severity reports should be filed in the open source data transfer tool's public GitHub repository, maintainer Daniel Stenberg said.

"Security researchers in doubt can still submit the issue on HackerOne and we can tell them what severity we deem it to be. Over the last few years, over 90 percent of all submissions could quickly be assessed to be less than HIGH."

Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty scheme this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team.

Stenberg has previously acknowledged that not all AI-assisted reports are bad, but the workload now demands another response.

"This policy change is entirely triggered by the current avalanche of vulnerability reports that keep pouring in. We see no end to them and we do not anticipate this flood to decrease within the next several months.

"We are struggling as a project as all key maintainers feel strained, overloaded and brought to the brink of what we can muster. We must act to survive. This is our next step in a survival strategy. It might not be our last. We aim to not drown."

Public handling would let more people assess reports, develop fixes, write advisories, and check for related problems before releases ship, Stenberg said.

Handling vulnerability reports publicly won't reduce the work per report, he admits, though it could spread the load and make the resulting lessons and documentation easier to find. At least that's the theory.

Public disclosure also gives attackers more time to exploit flaws before fixes arrive. The maintainer agrees this is unfortunate yet unavoidable.

"We limit this practice to less than HIGH for this reason: at least these problems are not terrible."

Stenberg said researchers using AI are generating unusual option combinations unlikely to occur in real applications, then treating minor discrepancies as vulnerabilities.

"We can't continue down this spiraling path with our sanity intact. We don't have the bandwidth, manpower or even will to handle a never-ending vulnerability reporting stream at this pace. I believe few software projects can stand this kind of prolonged high volume deluge for extended periods. Something needs to give way." ®

articles.title: US-designated terrorist Muhammad Sarwar dies in Lahore
articles.text:
Muhammad Sarwar, designated as a global terrorist by the US Treasury Department, died in Pakistan’s Lahore on Sunday.
“Pakistan Markazi Muslim League (PMML) Punjab President Muhammad Sarwar has passed away. He was on his way from home to the mosque to offer prayers when he collapsed and died,” a PMML spokesperson said in a statement.
The exact cause of his death has not been specified by PMML. However, 24NewsHD TV Channel reported that Sarwar died “due to a head injury sustained after falling down the stairs”.
PMML is a political offshoot of Mumbai attack mastermind Hafiz Saeed’s Jamaat-ud-Dawa. Saeed has been in Lahore’s Kot Lakhpat Jail since 2019 in multiple terror financing cases, for which he was convicted for multiple years, as per officials.
PMML leaders — Khalid Masood Sindhu, Saifullah Qasuri, Hafiz Talha Saeed, Yaqub Sheikh, Khalid Naik Gujjar, and Muzammil Iqbal Hashmi — expressed grief over the loss of their party leader.
“With the death of Muhammad Sarwar, the party has lost a strong and fearless leader,” said Muzammil Iqbal Hashmi.
Sarwar’s funeral was scheduled to be held at JuD headquarters, Jamia Al-Qadsia, in Lahore’s Chuburji area late on Sunday night.
In 2016, the US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated Sarwar and Shahid Mahmood, another senior Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) leader, as Specially Designated Global Terrorists (SDGTs).
The action was aimed at disrupting LeT’s fundraising and support networks. OFAC said the two men were designated for acting for or on behalf of the group, adding that all their property and interests in property subject to US jurisdiction were blocked.
“Sarwar and Mahmood of Lashkar-e-Taiba are responsible for raising and moving funds to support the terrorist group’s operations. The action not only aims to expose activities, but also disrupts Lashkar-e-Taiba’s financial network and ability to carry out violent terrorist attacks,” OFAC said at the time.
According to OFAC, Sarwar had been a senior LeT official in Lahore for more than 10 years and had held various leadership roles in the group. He had served as LeT’s Lahore chief since at least January 2015.
As the group’s Lahore chief, Sarwar maintained ties with its senior leaders. Between 2012 and 2013, he worked with LeT’s foreign affairs chief Hafiz Abdul Rahman Makki, who asked him for money to cover travel within Pakistan in early 2013, OFAC said.
Makki was designated by OFAC under Executive Order 13224 in November 2010.
Sarwar’s association with LeT dated back to the early 2000s. In his capacity as the group’s Lahore emir, he was directly involved in fundraising and used Pakistan’s formal financial system to raise and transfer funds on its behalf, OFAC said.
In 2008, Sarwar led delegations of businessmen to LeT facilities to solicit donations for the group. By mid-2009, he was one of two officials heading LeT’s finance wing in Lahore, according to OFAC.

articles.title: OneDrive loses bunch of Copilot shortcuts in File Explorer clear-out
articles.text:
Microsoft is pruning OneDrive's Copilot options from File Explorer's right-click menu, though the AI assistant isn't being shown the door entirely.

The Windows giant will remove shortcuts for summarizing documents, generating FAQs, comparing files and images, explaining images, extracting text, and asking questions. The rollout begins in mid-November and is expected to finish by early December. "Ask Copilot" will remain.

Microsoft's September 2025 announcement of the feature said: "We are bringing the power of AI directly into your daily file management experience. With just a few clicks, Copilot can help you summarize lengthy documents, generate an FAQ, compare files, or answer questions about your file."

Users can still right-click a OneDrive file and select "Ask Copilot" to start a conversation with the file attached, or use the Copilot icon in File Explorer Home. The individual actions will also remain available in the OneDrive activity center.

Adding a clutch of Copilot options with identical icons did little to make an already crowded menu easier to navigate. In its message on the subject, Microsoft said: "We're simplifying how people use Copilot with their OneDrive files in File Explorer."

An extra click, yes, but at least you won't need a taller screen to view even more context menu options.

Microsoft has stated that it intends to adopt a more thoughtful approach to how and where its AI assistant turns up in its product line. In March 2026, Windows boss Pavan Davuluri said: "We are reducing unnecessary Copilot entry points." File Explorer's crowded right-click menu seems as good a place to start as any.

The File Explorer context menu is also undergoing an overhaul as part of Microsoft's attempt to make it less "cluttered and sluggish," to the point where users could opt to have it work a bit like it used to in Windows 10. ®

articles.title: HPE to launch AI straight to the Moon
articles.text:
Forget space datacenters. Before the end of the year, HPE will have AI running on the Moon.

This isn’t some exec’s loony fantasy either. HPE has been building orbital compute platforms for the International Space Station (ISS) for years. Now, it’s sending its fourth-gen Spaceborne Computer to the Moon aboard Astrolab’s Flex Lunar Innovation Platform (FLIP) lunar rover.

Part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, the rover is set to be deployed near the Moon’s south pole by the Voyager Technologies Griffin-1 lander later this year.

Assuming a safe landing on the surface, FLIP will serve as a test bed for a range of emerging technologies including HPE’s latest space-faring compute platform.

Specifically, Spaceborne Computer 4, which for the sake of brevity we’ll just call SBC4, will carry out a number of AI and HPC-centric experiments during the rover’s year long mission on the lunar pole.

What we know about SBC4 so far

The actual silicon powering SBC4 is still a bit of a mystery. We’re told the reason for the secrecy largely comes down to the high-risk nature of the mission. If the hardware fails, HPE’s compute partner doesn’t want their name tied to it.

No guts but for the glory, we suppose, though Kioxia doesn't seem too worried.

What we do know is that it is equipped with a low-power central processing unit, a graphics processor, and will be equipped with a pair of mirrored Kioxia SSDs totaling 1 TB of capacity. That said, while it'll be among the most powerful computers on the Moon, it's still a pretty small system. The FLIP rover doesn't have an unlimited power or thermal budget. The rover's radiators can only dissipate so much heat.

Measuring in at around 5x10 inches and about an inch thick, while not a particularly big system, it's still large enough to house any number of existing compute platforms. For all we know, it could be powered by Nvidia’s GB10, AMD’s Xilinx Versal AI, or the guts of an old smartphone. We won't know until the thing powers up.

Less of a mystery is what SBC4 will be running and where. NASA plans to run a series of tuned LLM tests on the system, including a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) system to assist with searching and interpreting onboard documents. Additionally, the system will be tasked with running machine learning algorithms against camera and LiDAR data.

However, without knowing how large these LLMs are, it’s hard to infer the nature of the underlying hardware. We’re told to expect more details about the chips powering SBC4 once it’s up and running.

Alongside AI, SBC4 will also run several high performance computing (HPC) benchmarks designed to push the system to its limits. These benchmarks include high performance Linpack (HPL) and high performance conjugate gradient (HPCG), which means HPE and Astrolab will soon hold the distinction of the first Top500 submission made from a celestial body.

Not only do HPE’s systems power some of the fastest supercomputers on Earth, but they could soon hold the number one spot on the Moon — not that that’s a particularly high bar.

Beyond bragging rights, a workload like HPL could have other benefits like helping to keep the rover from icing over during the roughly 14-day-long night cycles the rover will repeatedly endure over the course of its mission.

Hardening SBC4 for the Moon

The Rover and by extension SBC4 will have to contend with extreme vibration stresses during launch and landing, wild temperature swings, not to mention cosmic rays and solar radiation since the Moon lacks the thick atmosphere and magnetic field that shields terrestrial compute.

But, as it turns out, radiation might not be as big a problem as you’d think. According to Fernandez, SBC4 is largely assembled from off-the-shelf components, including the solid state drives.

The compute platform is using standard Kioxia BG6 M.2 drives with the main line of protection being a software RAID 1.

“It’s a silent mirror. The boot order is to try this and if something has happened to it, go here,” Mark Fernandez, HPE’s chief scientist of space tech and solutions, explained. “With our nine years' experience in the Space Station using drives, we’ve even convinced them we don’t need to do anything special for space.”

However, this wasn’t always the thinking. As we reported at the time, early Spaceborne Computers suffered from high SSD failure rates. But as it turned out, so did the same drives deployed terrestrially. The cause of the failures wasn’t cosmic rays or energetic particles from the Sun, but rather bad capacitors, he explained. “I’ve had zero SSD failure since 2019.”

While off-the-shelf electronics are surprisingly radiation resistant — at least within FLIP’s mission parameters — HPE has invested heavily in software based redundancy and recovery.

Fernandez calls this “hardware hardening in software.” The idea being that the spare CPU cycles are used to continuously monitor and compare hardware metrics against a state table. If a parameter exceeds the specified threshold, SBC4 will take action to protect itself.

“At a high level, I say, I like to be running at full speed. I can't do that. I'll run at a slower speed. If I can't do that, I'd like to be booted, but not running anything, and then maybe the server will recover. And worst case, I'd like to be powered down rather than get destroyed,” he explained.

At the edge of the edge

FLIP is primarily intended as a proof of concept vehicle, which is to say it’s a test bed for technologies that may eventually find their way to the Moon on other missions.

The inclusion of SBC4 reflects the realities of operating at the far edge of Earth’s orbit. The latency between Earth and the Moon is nowhere near as bad as Mars's up to 44 minute round-trip communication time, but even 2.5 seconds makes real-time control from Houston, or in this case Astrolab’s mission control, which by the way is also powered by HPE's Greenlake Private Cloud stack, in Hawthorne, California a bit unwieldy.

Further complicating matters is the bandwidth afforded the rover. When Artemis 2 traveled around the Moon earlier this year, astronauts weren’t able to send back high-res photographs in real time due to the lack of bandwidth. It was only after the mission was on its way back to Earth that they were able to establish a big enough pipe to transmit the full-res images.

For this reason, SBC4 is designed to operate “at the edge of the edge,” Fernandez said.

Given the bandwidth constraints, it’s far easier to process as much of the data and telemetry gathered by the rover’s array of cameras, lidars, and environmental sensors locally.

“It’s important to ship back insight to Earth rather than all the raw data whenever possible. So having the edge compute capability to process the raw data locally, save on bandwidth back to Earth,” Astrolab CEO Jaret Matthews said.

Matthews isn’t the only one to share this perspective. Earlier this year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang described the challenges and opportunities of space-based computing with analysts during the company’s Q1 earnings call.

"There are many different computing problems that really want to be done in space," he said at the time. "One of the best use cases of GPUs in space is imaging. To be able to do imaging at very large, very high resolutions, extremely large scales and very, very fast, it's hard to do that by sending petabytes and petabytes of imaging data back here on Earth and doing that work, it's easier just to do it out in space."

Though others' ambitions are far greater. Google, Amazon, and SpaceX are all touting orbital datacenters powered by the Sun as the answer to terrestrial power constraints — Elon Musk wants you to believe he'll eventually be manufacturing deep-space datacenters on the Moon and lobbing them into the far reaches of the solar system using mass drivers — the economics of getting those bit barns into low Earth orbit remain unproven and so far unviable.

Despite this, executives and administrators at HPE, Astrolab, Kioxia, and NASA believe that space-based datacenters are still feasible long term.

FLIP

HPE’s Spaceborne Computer 4 will be one of several payloads aboard the FLIP rover.

FLIP will be the largest rover launched by the US since the Apollo program’s manned Moon buggy. And it is by no means small. Designed by Astrolab while measuring roughly 7 feet (2.13 meters) in length and weighing about half a ton, the rover is packed to the gills with cameras, sensors, and even a projector which will eventually be used in place of LCDs on future manned missions to the lunar surface.

For FLIP’s purposes, it’ll mostly be used to project partners' logos onto the Moon’s surface as a sorta advertising gimmick to keep the lights on back at Astrolab’s facilities in Hawthorne while it works on its FLEX rover, which Matthews characterizes as a sort of F150 or Caterpillar tractor for the Moon.

Beyond the scientific equipment, solar panels, and radiators, arguably FLIP’s most striking feature is its disproportionately large wheels. Developed by Venturi Space, along with the rover’s battery pack, these wheels are designed to function much like a pneumatic tire, just without air or rubber. Their size is also intentional. The same wheels found on FLIP are intended for use on NASA’s CLV-1 rover, which is slated to launch in 2028.

Much like FLIP offers HPE as a proving ground to test its lunar compute platform, the rover will do the same for Venturi’s wheels.

Spaceborne Computer 4 and FLIP are slated to launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket later this year and will fly to the Moon’s south pole by Astrobotic’s Griffin-1 lander.

Griffin is classified as a medium class lander measuring roughly 15 feet around and 6.5 feet tall (that’s about 4.5 and 2 meters for those of you living in a nation civilized enough to use metric outside the sciences).

The lander is equipped with seven main engines responsible for everything from trans-lunar injection, trajectory correction, lunar orbit insertion, and powered descent to the surface. Four clusters of attitude control thrusters, meanwhile, will (hopefully) keep the thing pointed the right way up.

FLIP is expected to touch down near the Mons Mouton area along the edge of the South Pole before the end of the year. ®

articles.title: Trump admin ‘withholding’ approval for Europe-funded Patriot missiles for Ukraine—WaPo report
articles.text:
New Delhi: The Trump administration has withheld approval for sending crucial Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine, according to a report by The Washington Post report published Tuesday, leaving Kyiv vulnerable to ongoing Russian missile and drone strikes.
This delay comes amid US President Donald Trump’s recent public criticism of Ukraine and a marked change in his stance toward Russia.
Unlike previous debates in Washington over multi-billion-dollar military aid packages funded by US taxpayers, the current bottleneck involves weapons that have already been bought and paid for. European allies and the Ukrainian government have utilised billions in cleared funds through NATO frameworks to secure the interceptors. However, the transfers remain subject to US authorisation.
The bottleneck can be traced to US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who has neither formally rejected the transfers nor taken the necessary steps to authorise them. By withholding his signature on essential agreement documents, Hegseth has stalled deliveries without openly announcing a policy shift.
The weapons are being purchased through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) framework, which allows European allies to fund the purchase of American military supplies for Kyiv without drawing on US taxpayer funds. Multiple countries including Germany, Norway and the Netherlands have pooled financial resources to purchase American military equipment.
However, since Patriot PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptors are manufactured in the US by RTX and Lockheed Martin, international partners cannot transfer them without Washington’s approval. This applies to both new factory orders and re-export requests from European inventories.
The delay comes as Ukraine faces a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted that monthly deliveries of the missiles from the US have been throttled to approximately 12 units, or a fourth of the prior supply rate. A Ukrainian official told The Washington Post last Thursday that Kyiv’s reserves had dwindled to just “a couple” of functional interceptors, leaving its air defences critically strained.
Global availability of Patriot interceptors has also come under pressure from ongoing military engagements in West Asia. The Pentagon has signalled to Congress its intention to divert roughly $750 million in partner-provided PURL funding away from Kyiv to replenish depleted US stockpiles of THAAD and Patriot systems.
On Monday, Zelenskyy put out a video appeal to US senators where he talked about the deliberate slowdown of missile shipments being leveraged to discourage Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian oil-refining infrastructure.
These tensions are further compounded by efforts in Washington to soften specific sanctions on Russian fuel exports, highlighting a rift between American energy objectives and Ukraine’s defensive strategy.
Seeking to resolve the deadlock, Zelenskyy announced on his official Telegram channel Tuesday that he had held what he described as a “substantive” and “constructive” call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Beyond the stalled Patriot deliveries, the dialogue touched upon wider security concerns, including a suspension of American early-warning tracking intelligence and bandwidth restrictions affecting Starlink and military Starshield satellite communications.
However, the State Department lacks the regulatory authority to override Pentagon export restrictions. While Rubio kept communication channels open, Washington has continued to press Kyiv towards diplomatic negotiations with Moscow.
The operational impact of the delays has been compounded by Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Recent strikes severed electricity access for over 500,000 households across the Kyiv region, underscoring the consequences of Ukraine’s strained air-defence capabilities.
The delays have also prompted political opposition on Capitol Hill, where congressional leaders are questioning the administration’s handling of the situation. During an official press interaction Monday, Representative Rosa DeLauro, Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Committee, criticised Hegseth’s administrative hold, arguing that using bureaucratic procedures to stall shipments undermines confidence among global allies.
This legislative backlash contrasts with Trump’s position on continued aid to Kyiv.
The US President has reiterated his scepticism towards ongoing assistance to Ukraine, telling news outlets that Ukraine has “given nothing to us”, while asserting that withholding weapons transfers could provide leverage to push both nations towards peace talks.

New Delhi: Indian Air Force chief, Air Chief Marshal AP Singh, who superannuates at the end of this month, Tuesday completed his final flying sortie in the the HJT-16 Kiran Mk-1 trainer aircraft, bringing his flying career to a close.
The 55 minute sortie was done with his first flying instructor, Wing Commander V. S. Kochar (Retd), in an aircraft bearing tail number U-707.
It marked a reunion between instructor and student, reconnecting the Chief of the Air Staff (CAS) with the beginning of his flying journey in the force on 28 January 1984.
More than four decades later, today’s sortie in the Kiran brought his flying journey in the IAF full circle.
The occasion was a tribute to the rich tradition of flying training in the Indian Air Force and to the invaluable role played by flying instructors in nurturing generations of air warriors, the IAF said in a statement.
The return to the Kiran, an iconic trainer aircraft associated with the training of IAF pilots, added special significance to the sortie.
The presence of Wg Cdr V. S. Kochar (Retd), who had guided the CAS during his earliest flying days, made the occasion especially meaningful, bringing together memories of the CAS’s first flight and the culmination of his flying journey in IAF aircraft, the IAF said.

articles.title: Pakistan-Somalia ‘JF-17 deal’: Islamabad’s expanding footprint in Africa
articles.text:
New Delhi: Last week, Somalia reached an agreement with Pakistan to acquire JF-17 Thunder multirole fighter aircraft as part of efforts to rebuild and modernise its air force, according to Turkish news outlet TRHaber.
The report did not specify the number of aircraft Somalia intends to purchase, the value of the deal, or when deliveries are expected to begin. If concluded, this acquisition would mark Mogadishu’s largest defence procurement since the collapse of the central government in 1991.
The development comes weeks after a senior Pakistan Air Force (PAF) delegation visited Mogadishu for talks on rebuilding Somalia’s air force and expanding defence and air-defence cooperation between the two countries.
The delegation was led by Air Marshal Muhammad Sarfraz, Pakistan’s Air Defence Commander and Deputy Chief of the Air Staff. During the visit, he held meetings with senior Somali officials, including President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre and Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi.
Air Marshal Sarfraz also met Brigadier General Abdirisaaq Mahmoud Haji, the commander of the Somali Air Force, at the force’s headquarters. Their discussions focused on pilot and personnel training, institutional development, specialised skills and the capabilities required to rebuild and strengthen Somalia’s air force.
According to reports and images from the meetings, Air Marshal Sarfraz presented the Somali Air Force commander with a model of the JF-17 Thunder. At the time, however, neither side announced an agreement for Somalia to purchase the aircraft.
Somalia was previously reported in February to be in discussions with Pakistan over the possible acquisition of JF-17 fighter aircraft, jointly produced by Pakistan and China.
The September visit followed a trip to Pakistan the previous month by a Somali delegation led by Defence Minister Fiqi, during which they met Field Marshal Asim Munir. Islamabad and Mogadishu agreed to deepen bilateral defence and security cooperation.
In August, they signed an MoU in Islamabad for cooperation in counterterrorism, military training, the exchange of expertise and broader military capacity building.
Neither side then said whether the agreement included the purchase of fighter aircraft or other major weapons systems.
Seen in the context of Pakistan’s increasing engagement in West Asia—it signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in August, and Pakistan–Saudi Arabia defence agreement last year—the reported deal with the African country becomes significant.
It also came amid an increasingly fluid geopolitical environment—from the Gulf and the Red Sea to the Horn of Africa—and at a time when Somalia seeks new partners to rebuild its security institutions after more than three decades of domestic conflict.
Domestically, Somalia is fighting Al-Shabaab, the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group that continues to operate across parts of southern and central Somalia and carry out attacks against government and civilian targets. The country has also been attempting to rebuild its armed forces and establish greater control over its territory and airspace.
Against that backdrop, the Pakistan-Somalia agreement offers Islamabad an opportunity to extend its military partnerships into the Horn of Africa, and gives Mogadishu access to a country willing to offer military expertise, and potentially weapons.
The Pakistan-Somali defence cooperation is also being watched closely by analysts from New Delhi, given it may allow Islamabad logistics leverage in a region becoming increasingly significant for maritime trade.
Former Indian ambassador Gurjit Singh sees the agreement as part of a wider Pakistani strategy. “Pakistan is attempting to convert its long-standing military relationships with Muslim countries into a wider network of strategic partnerships, while simultaneously turning its defence industry into an instrument of foreign policy”, he told ThePrint.
“Somalia is especially important because it extends that network from the Gulf into the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea,” he added.
Also read: The curious case of Pakistan’s JF-17 ‘orders’
Why Horn of Africa significant & where Pakistan fits
Somalia occupies an important geographic position. Its coastline stretches along the Gulf of Aden and the western Indian Ocean, giving it a strategic location near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which has emerged as one of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, especially as Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted since the US/Israel-Iran war broke out in February.
The Bab al-Mandab Strait connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean and is vital to energy supplies and global commercial shipping.
That geography gives Somalia importance much beyond its military capabilities. For Pakistan, establishing a closer defence relationship with Mogadishu can, therefore, extend its diplomatic and security reach from the Gulf into East Africa, while following the footsteps of Saudi and Turkey.
Pakistan is attempting to convert its long-standing military relationships with Muslim countries into a wider network of strategic partnerships, while simultaneously turning its defence industry into an instrument of foreign policy—Former ambassador Gurjit Singh.
Moreover, Pakistan seems to follow the lead of its closest allies in spreading its influence in African Muslim countries, invoking history, religion and strategic ties. Pakistan currently is the largest market for Turkey’s arms, accounting for roughly 16 percent of total Turkish defense exports. Pakistan also maintains close relations with Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
However, it is no secret that Pakistan’s relations with the United Arab Emirates are in decline, partly due to the UAE’s growing ties with India and Islamabad’s growing alignment with the Saudis.
The Islamabad-Abu Dhabi ties have also been negatively impacted by Pakistan signing the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, and Pakistan–Saudi Arabia defence agreement, both involving Saudis.
Pakistan & Somalia—as seen from Saudi Arabia
For Saudi Arabia, Somalia is the road to reshape the security order around the Red Sea and counter the UAE influence and Iran-aligned threats.
According to an April 2026 report by Dr John Calabrese, a former director of East-Asia Project (MAP) of Washington-based think tank Middle East Institute, Somalia is no longer a peripheral concern for Riyadh. “It has become a key arena where Gulf rivalry, maritime insecurity, and Saudi ambitions converge.”
It is driven mainly by Saudi’s growing rift with the UAE. Abu Dhabi already has a footprint in Somalia since 2010 having trained security forces, securing long-term port management and development concessions in areas like Berbera and Bosaso and having cultivated political ties with Somaliland and Puntland.
Riyadh is more concerned about Abu Dhabi’s bypassing of Somalia’s Saudi-backed federal government and empowering sub-State actors.
To counter it, Saudi is now positioning itself as the champion of Somalian sovereignty and territorial integrity and has hence aligned more with the capital. This has another aim— it establishes Saudi as the defining Gulf player in the Horn of Africa committed more to state authority than just a transactional partnership like the UAE.
Somalia has a coastline along the Gulf of Aden, a critical maritime corridor linking the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea (through Bab-al Mandab) and the Suez Canal. This is the site of one quarter of the global container trade transit route, significant to all external players including Pakistan—and India.
If you look at maritime positioning, I don’t think Pakistan is major naval power, and it is unlikely to become one. It is also not going to play a major role in policing the waters. The main significance, then, is logistics—strategic affairs expert Ilya Roubanis.
Amid the West Asia war, Iran-backed Houthis have wreaked havoc on shipping lines and there are reports of the Houthis now cooperating with the al-Shabaab. For Saudi, the Somalian coastline risks becoming the link to enable coordination on both sides of Bab al-Mandab.
Al-Shabaab networks in East Africa have helped funnel arms from Iran and regional routes through maritime channels earlier. Despite deep ideological differences (al-Shabaab is Sunni Islamist while Houthis belong to the Zaydi branch of Shia Islam), both groups cooperate due to mutual hostility toward Western nations, Israel, and regional governments.
With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed due to the ongoing war, Saudi re-routes its exports through the Red Sea and hence Somalia has become strategically important for multiple reasons, linking the coastline with Riyadh’s economic standpoint.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia’s Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement of September 2025—committed to mutual defence, and expanding military cooperation——could give both countries greater leverage in Somalia.
However, the defence cooperation is not likely to suddenly make Pakistan a major naval actor in the strategically significant region.
“A lot of the Pakistani Navy’s hardware is co-produced with Turkey, which already has a military base in Somalia, and it is also developing another base in Sudan. So, I think one element here is complementarity. The other thing to watch is the broader regional picture,” strategic affairs expert Ilya Roubanis told ThePrint.
Expanding further he added that Somalia is a weak state, and there is already a significant presence of outside powers in the region. Israel has recognised Somaliland, while the UAE has logistical capabilities that allow it to participate in the war in Sudan, whereas Saudi Arabia supports the opposite side — the Sudanese government.
Pakistan has historically tried to balance between the UAE and Saudi Arabia.
“If you look at the maritime positioning, I don’t think Pakistan is a major naval power, and it is unlikely to become one. It is also not going to play a major role in policing the waters. The main significance, then, is logistics: the ability to deliver troops on the ground if they are needed, as well as providing logistical support. That appears to shadow Saudi interests and provide a potential deployment capability if and when Saudi Arabia needs it,” he added.
Turkey and Saudi play the strategic game together. But Ankara’s interests in Somalia are not the same as Saudi’s. For Ankara, it is the abundance of oil deposits which drives President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s interest.
In a May 2026 article, UK based security think tank RUSI argued Erdogan enjoys widespread popularity in the region owing to his humanitarian aid and soft diplomacy. In 2011, he was the first non-African head of state to visit Somalia in 20 years.
According to RUSI, Ankara is now Mogadishu’s “foremost foreign ally”, with Turkish companies also assuming control of the management of the Mogadishu port and airport, and Somalia hosting Ankara’s largest overseas military base– Camp Turksom—since 2017.
Though a NATO member, Turkey has often taken an assertive independent position across West Asia, North Africa and the Horn of Africa. The promise of oil and gas is what is enticing to Ankara, which signed a deal with Somalia in 2024. Recent studies cited by RUSI say the region has around 30 billion barrels of oil, a quarter of the UAE’s current crude oil reserves.
There is also a hydrocarbon deal, under which Turkey’s latest deepwater drillship, the Çağrı Bey, came to Mogadishu Port, its first trip beyond Turkey’s own waters, in April.
With the current West Asia crisis disrupting global supply, Somalia, thus, becomes crucial for Turkey.
Turkey’s homegrown military technology—Jets, drones, helicopters, warships and more—have appeared in Mogadishu and played a role in operations against al-Shabaab.
According to a RUSI analysis, Somalia is emerging as a broader platform for Türkiye to project its influence. This was underscored by Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s visit to Türkiye on 30 December 2025, his first foreign trip after Israel unilaterally recognised Somaliland in late December.
During that trip, the two sides agreed on plans for a Turkish military base at Laas Qoray, in a disputed part of Somalia along the Gulf of Aden. A Turkish base at Laas Qoray would amount to a direct counterweight to the expanding Israeli and Emirati presence in Somaliland farther along the coast.
In this backdrop, ambassador Singh said the Pakistan–Somalia agreement should not be viewed as an isolated bilateral arrangement after the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
In his view, there is therefore a potentially important security chain emerging.
“The Pakistani-Somali relationship can therefore become an extension of this wider security ecosystem rather than a conventional arms relationship. I would describe this not yet as a formal alliance system, but as an emerging web of overlapping security partnerships,” he added.
Roubanis argues that Saudi Arabia may be the most important lens to understand Pakistan’s interest in Somalia.
Saudi Arabia does not have a major expeditionary force. Turkey does, but it would be reluctant to deploy its own troops and expose Turkish forces to the risks involved, he said.
Pakistan, on the other hand, has deployed forces on behalf of Saudi Arabia in several places and has played a role, particularly through its special forces. Pakistan does not have a major expeditionary force, and it does not have major maritime interests in the region, Somalia is an important source of sailors for the international merchant fleet, but Pakistan itself is not a naval power, he said.
Somalia is, therefore, an auxiliary. “Pakistan has, therefore, always been viewed as a force that is available and ready to deploy in support of Saudi interests. My interpretation is that Pakistan is there because Saudi Arabia asked it to be there,” he added.
(Edited by Ajeet Tiwari)

articles.title: Bharat Rice for troops: Army taps FCI warehouses to boost military logistics after Operation Sindoor
articles.text:
New Delhi: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh has launched the Bharat Rice initiative for the Indian Army at an event, where the Army also signed a five-year memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Food Corporation of India (FCI) to strengthen military logistics during operational contingencies.
The Bharat Rice initiative is intended to streamline the supply of rice to troops, particularly those stationed in remote areas of Ladakh and the North East.
Bharat Rice was originally introduced by the government in February 2024 as part of its broader Bharat Brand range of essential commodities to provide consumers with rice at subsidised prices.
The event was attended by Army chief Staff General Dhiraj Seth, Minister of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution Pralhad Joshi, and representatives of FCI and the National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation of India Limited (NAFED).
Under the new arrangement, rice will be delivered directly to Army supply depots instead of requiring individual depots to collect their allocations from local FCI facilities. The initiative is intended to streamline distribution, particularly to troops deployed in remote and forward areas.
The rice will be supplied in 10-kg and 30-kg bags. The smaller packaging formats are intended to make handling and transportation easier in difficult terrain.
The Department of Food and Public Distribution has allocated 1.25 lakh metric tonnes of rice for the Army, according to the details provided for the initiative. The allocation and delivery schedule will determine how the arrangement is implemented across the Army’s supply network.
The rice will be supplied through an institutional arrangement involving NAFED and will be custom-milled according to prescribed defence specifications. Quality checks are intended to ensure that the rice is free from foreign matter and admixtures, with limits on broken, damaged and discoloured grains.
The supply arrangement is scheduled for the financial year 2026–27. Its implementation follows 18 months of coordination among the Army, FCI, NAFED and the Department of Food and Public Distribution.
Five-year logistics agreement
Separately, the five-year MoU between the Army and FCI establishes a framework for the military to use identified FCI warehousing infrastructure, manpower and material-handling equipment during operational contingencies. The agreement can be extended by mutual consent.
The arrangement will allow the Army to incorporate civilian logistics infrastructure into its operational plans, including for additional storage, rapid mobilisation and the forward positioning of supplies closer to operational areas.
The agreement draws on lessons from Operation Sindoor, highlighting the need for resilient supply chains that can respond to contingencies arising at short notice and continuing over extended periods. It also reflects a broader government approach to coordinating civilian infrastructure and military requirements, in line with the objectives of the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan.
The defence ministry has also highlighted other Army welfare and modernisation measures, including specialised nutritional rations for newly inducted Agniveer recruits, greater standardisation of ration scales across the three armed forces, and proposals to introduce organic rations at forward locations.

articles.title: Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit is new IAF chief, first Mirage-2000 pilot to head force
articles.text:
New Delhi: Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, Vice-Chief of the Indian Air Force (IAF), will take over as the next Chief of the Air Staff on 31 October.
He will assume command of the IAF from Air Chief Marshal A.P.Singh who will superannuate that day.
An Experimental Test Pilot and Qualified Flying Instructor with more than 3,500 hours of flying experience, Dixit will be the first officer to have commanded a Mirage-2000 squadron to go on to become the IAF chief.
His appointment is significant as he belongs to a generation of fighter pilots that came of age with the induction of the Mirage-2000 into the IAF and the evolution of modern air warfare, including beyond-visual-range (BVR) combat. The warfighting is now increasingly about beyond visual range tactics and capabilities.
Dixit was commissioned into the IAF’s fighter stream on 6 December 1986. He is an alumnus of the National Defence Academy, the Defence Staff Services College in Bangladesh, and the National Defence College.
A keen observer of the changing nature of aerial warfare, Dixit has spoken candidly about the growing role of unmanned systems and their integration with manned aircraft.
In May, while serving as the Chief of Integrated Defence Staff (CISC), Dixit said that the robotic warfare of the future was already here and that unmanned aerial systems were no longer merely enablers but means of warfare in their own right.
Unmanned aircraft were “already replacing manned aircraft in an increasing variety of roles” and were influencing the outcome of conflicts, he asserted.
Apart from the Mirage-2000, Dixit has extensive flying experience on a range of aircraft, including the Mirage-2000, various MiG variants, HPT-32, An-32, Avro, Kiran, Jaguar, IL-78, Hawk and Tejas.
During his nearly four-decade career, he has been involved in several operations and exercises, including Operation Safed Sagar, Operation Rakshak, Cope India and Operation Sindoor.
As Commanding Officer, Dixit re-equipped No. 9 Squadron with the Mirage-2000 and later commanded a frontline fighter air base in the Western Sector as well as a premier fighter training base in the Southern Sector. He has also served as Directing Staff at the Air Force Test Pilots School and as Principal Director, Air Staff Requirement, at Air Headquarters.
Dixit subsequently served as Air Defence Commander of Southern Air Command and held key appointments including Assistant Chief of the Air Staff (Projects), Assistant Chief of the Air Staff (Plans), Senior Air Staff Officer at Headquarters South Western Air Command and Deputy Chief of the Air Staff at Air Headquarters.
As CISC, Dixit pushed for greater jointness and integration among the three services. During his tenure, multiple joint doctrines and orders were issued and several initiatives were undertaken to strengthen the armed forces’ capabilities across domains.
