articles.title: Hindustan Shipyard delivers Surya, 1st of 5 logistics vessels to boost Navy’s high-seas endurance
articles.text:
Hyderabad: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh Tuesday commissioned the first of the five indigenous Fleet Support Ships (FSS-1), Surya, at Hindustan Shipyard Limited (HSL) in Visakhapatnam, marking a critical evolutionary step in the Navy’s operational reach across the Indian Ocean Region (IOR).
The vessel was built with one clear role: to replenish frontline warships at sea with fuel, water, ammunition, and other essential stores, to bolster naval endurance. It fundamentally increases the Navy’s capacity to fight longer and harder at sea without returning to port, Chief of the Naval Staff, Admiral Krishna Swaminathan said, during the launch.
With a displacement of approximately 43,500 tonnes DWT (deadweight tonnage), Surya entered the water of the Bay of Bengal at Vizag just 18 months after steel cutting, a feat for the once-bootstrapped Hindustan Shipyard Limited. Steel cutting marks the official beginning of the shipbuilding lifecycle.
HSL has been commissioned and contracted by the Navy to build five Fleet Support Ships at a cost of Rs 19,500 crore, a Press Bureau of India statement said.
Launched the first indigenous Fleet Support Ship ‘INS Surya’ at Hindustan Shipyard Ltd in Visakhapatnam. The launch of FSS1 is a symbol of achievement, keel laying of FSS5 is a symbol of resolve and the new Slipway is a symbol of our growing capability. HSL is fast emerging as a… pic.twitter.com/xH3kfJHOEm
— Rajnath Singh (@rajnathsingh) October 6, 2026
Built to defend herself and support warships in replenishing themselves, Surya also has a helicopter deck that can accommodate multi-role helicopters. Her fit includes AK 630 guns, the Kavach decoy system, the marines torpedo defence system, and electronic warfare suites named Shakti, and Sea King 42 Charlie helicopters. Surya is a large vessel—223.6 metres long and 31.5 metres wide—equipped with two main engines of 2 MW each to help her sail at a top speed of 20 knots, according to details provided by HSL at the time of launch.
According to the PIB statement, the launch of the FSS-1 was coupled with the inauguration of a 300-tonne Goliath Crane and lengthened Slipway-4, which would not just assist HSL in larger constructions, but also cement the public sector undertaking (PSU) as a premier tier-one defence shipbuilder.
Speaking at the launch of the FSS-1, the defence minister applauded the transformation of Hindustan Shipyard from a financially distressed unit to an operationally functional Category-I Miniratna PSU.
“In 2025, we categorised Hindustan Shipyard as a Miniratna PSU and ensured it was financially restored. Today, HSL is part of an Integrated National Maritime Ecosystem, being part of the Eastern Naval Command, the Naval Dockyard, and the Visakhapatnam Port. As part of India’s maritime Vision 2030, I would like Hindustan Shipyard to team up with DRDO, Academia, industry, MSMEs, and start-ups to work together as an integrated team,” Rajnath Singh said.
The 85-year-old HSL was burdened by decades of negative net worth and operational inefficiencies dating back to the 1980s. For decades, it suffered from limited naval order flows and execution delays after shifting to the Ministry of Defence (MoD) in 2010.
However, after a sustained financial bailout from the Centre, HSL turned out financially and operationally, finally tripling its turnover in FY 2024, recording sales of Rs 1,400 crore from just about Rs 478 crore in FY21. In the last few years, the PSU was able to scale its order books significantly past Rs 20,000 crore, propelled by major projects like the Navy Fleet Support Ships. Earlier in August, HSL delivered the Navy-commissioned INS Nipun, the second indigenous Nistar-class Diving Support Vessel (DSV).
Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, Chief of the Naval Staff, said the FSS was critical for the Navy’s Blue Water Fleet. “It grants us three operational advantages: longer endurance, greater reach, and faster response in the Indian Ocean Region (IOR). These vessels will also be useful in humanitarian assistance, disaster relief, personnel evacuation, and help us respond in other emergencies.”
The vessel sails with a complement of 215 personnel and can carry about 20,000 tonnes of diesel, 2,500 tonnes of aviation fuel, and about 1,000 tonnes of fresh water for transfer to other ships at sea. It is equipped to also carry solid stores of provisions and coal, amounting to nearly 240 tonnes, HSL officials said during the launch.
The Chairman & Managing Director (CMD) of HSL, Rear Admiral C. Raghuram, VSM (Retd.), highlighted the historic nature of achieving three massive shipyard milestones simultaneously. At the launch of FSS-1, he said, “Two warships commissioned, a record year, and now three milestones in a single day,” referring to INS Nipun, the FSS-1, and the launch of the Goliath crane and the Slipway-4.
Rear Admiral Raghuram took over as CMD of Hindustan Shipyard Limited in July to help steer and expand HSL’s submarine and warship manufacturing capabilities.
HSL was established in 1941 as Scindia Shipyard by Walchand Hirachand in Visakhapatnam, with the foundation stone laid by Dr Rajendra Prasad, who later became India’s first President. Even before it was incorporated as a public limited company in 1951, the shipyard built Jal Usha, the country’s first modern ocean-going steamship built completely in independent India.
Later, in 1961, it was nationalised by the Indian government and renamed Hindustan Shipyard Limited.

articles.title: Asim Munir reshuffles his Corps Commanders. But three-star generals rarely leave the system in Pakistan
articles.text:
New Delhi: The Pakistan Army has reshuffled its senior command structure with the elevation of several Major Generals to Lieutenant Generals while also making new appointments to key Corps Commander-level positions.
This was made public immediately after the 277th Corps Commanders’ conference held in Rawalpindi on 2 October.
Analysts are looking at potential ramifications on Pakistan’s internal political and security landscape and the Pakistan Army’s posture vis-a-vis India. Most appointments, however, are routine.
That Field Marshal Asim Munir has picked officers based on his preference is not surprising; every Army Chief strives to do the same.
Munir’s Corps Commanders
For 11 Corps, Peshawar, Mohammed Naeem Akhtar from the Azad Kashmir Regiment has been selected. He has replaced Lt Gen Omar Ahmed Bukhari, 22 Baloch Regiment, who has now been given the post of Chief of General Staff, a highly coveted post after the Chief of the Army Staff (COAS).
The Peshawar-based XI corps is closely watched, for it is not only among the army’s key field formations, but those heading it typically assume a bigger public role. It also sees a greater degree of activity, liaisons more closely with the ISI, and has a larger footprint in civilian affairs since its commander sits on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Provincial Apex Committee. The logic, hence, goes that those who are selected to head this corps are tapped for bigger roles in the future.
Umar Bashir, Artillery, has been made Corps Commander, 4 Corps, Lahore, by Field Marshal Asim Munir.
Field Marshal Asim Munir has appointed Lt Gen Shakirullah Khattak, Armoured Corps (13 Lancers) who was chairman, Heavy Industries, Taxila, the new Corps Commander at Mangla, or the I Corps. This follows a recent convention of sending either armoured corps or artillery officers there.
Khattak will be replacing Lt Gen Nauman Zakaria, who was also an Armoured Corps officer. While being the commander of I corps, Zakaria was simultaneously heading the newly established Army Rocket Force Command (ARFC), announced by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in August 2025. He captured headlines at this year’s Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore in May. Though he leaves the I Corps, there has been no reported change of guard for the ARFC.
The Mangla Corps deals with Pakistan’s eastern border—India. It has historically had three Infantry divisions, and one Armoured Division under it, positioned at Jhelum, Kharian and Mangla.
Rana Banerji, who headed the Pakistan desk at R&AW, in a monograph dated September 2013 writes: “After the 2003 ceasefire on the Line of Control (LOC), one of these divisions was temporarily deployed to the Western sector, to assist XI Corps, Peshawar in counter-insurgency (COIN) operations against tribal insurgencies in Swat and FATA.” Presently, the Mangla Corps retains its armoured components alongside infantry and mechanised infantry divisions.
Field Marshal Asim Munir has appointed Mohammad Amer Najam, 19 Sind Regiment, who was serving as inspector general, training and evaluation at General Headquarters, as corps commander, 2 Corps, Multan. The I Corps Mangla, along with II Corps Multan, forms the Pakistan Army’s Strike Corps.
Lieutenant General Inayat Hussain, Frontier Force Regiment, hitherto chief of logistics staff at GHQ, has been appointed the new corps commander, 12 Corps, Quetta by Field Marshal Asim Munir.
Among three-star appointments, including at the corps-commander level, the Army Chief strives for ensuring representation from all major arms (Armoured Corps, Infantry, Artillery, Engineers, Air Defence) to maintain institutional equity and cohesion across the service.
Three-star ranks never retire
According to Rana Banerji’s column for Rediff, at least six lieutenant generals of the 80th Pakistan Military Academy long courses, who were due for retirement after completing four years in this rank, may now be phased out.
These include Lt Gen Inam Haider Malik (Engineers, Chairman, National Disaster Management Authority) and Lt Gen Fayyaz Hussain Shah (Sind Regiment, Corps Commander, 4 Corps, Lahore); Lt Gen Muhammad Zafar Iqbal (Air Defence, commander, Air Defence Command, Rawalpindi); Lt Gen Shahid Imtiaz (Azad Kashmir Regiment, Military Secretary); Lt Gen Ahsan Gulrez (Frontier Force Regiment, Corps Commander, 2 Corps, Multan) and Lt Gen Nauman Zakaria (Armoured Corps, Corps Commander, 1 Corps, Mangla).
Formally, three-star generals in Pakistan do retire. In practice, retirement doesn’t equal being out of the army’s orbit. They only move out of General Headquarters (GHQ), Rawalpindi, into positions that the high command at GHQ continues to shape.
Take the example of Lt General Nauman Mahmood (Retd), who was appointed as the first secretary general of the Makkah Defence Alliance in September 2026. He had notably commanded the XI Corps, Peshawar and his tenure had coincided with one of the most sensitive periods along Pakistan’s western border, witnessing the withdrawal of the United States from Afghanistan.
A 2018 study by Paul Staniland et al., shows that retired corps commanders rarely enter electoral politics. There is an “institutionalised transmission belt that shifts retired elites into military-owned charitable foundations and affiliated corporations, posts in the civilian government, and other positions of real and/or symbolic authority”.
These positions, labeled “off-ramps”, provide officers strong incentives to toe the organisational line while serving and to avoid directly participating in politics after retirement, the study adds. More so as for most of the Pakistani military elite, their first corps command is their last major command.
There’s the Water and Power Development Authority (WAPDA) that is chaired by a retired Lt Gen—Muhammad Saeed—who had earlier served as the CGS and corps commander of 5-Corps Karachi. Even Pakistan’s National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) has more or less been headed by a three-star level officer.
However, the dominant post-retirement slot is a blend of foundations and associated corporations led by the military—and for the military, such as the Fauji Foundation and its subsidiaries, Army Welfare Trust and Defence Housing Authority.
Ayesha Siddiqa, in her seminal work Military Inc., termed the military’s deep penetration into Pakistan’s economy as ‘Milbus’ (Military-Business).
Fauji Foundation is headed by a retired lieutenant general—Anwar Ali Hyder. The governing body of the Defence Housing Authority (DHA) is chaired by Lt Gen Muhammad Ali (Retd) who is also the Secretary Defence, Ministry of Defence. DHA acquires land for real estate purposes to provide premier housing to the military fraternity, which has resulted in the army being known as Pakistan’s “biggest land grabber”.
The post-retirement trajectory of three-star generals reinforces that Pakistan is not a state with an army, but rather its army has a state to itself.
Pakistan’s intelligence chiefs
Last month, ThePrint reported on the Pakistan Army carrying out a series of new appointments at the two-star level. Most notable was a change in command of Director General-Military Intelligence (DG-MI), now assigned to Major General Adil Iftikhar Warraich.
This post matters because it is a stepping stone, given the convention of DG-MI ascending to the head of ISI. Take the example of the incumbent army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, who served as the head of MI and ISI both, later bagging the biggest post of army chief.
If DG-MI’s appointment was noteworthy last month, then the one-year extension given to the DG ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence)—Lt Gen Asim Malik—who has been serving the post since September 2024 stands out.
(Edited by Viny Mishra)

articles.title: Delhi govt to recruit 15,000 more home guard personnel: LG
articles.text: New Delhi: The Delhi government will recruit 15,000 home guards, taking their total number to 25,000, an official statement said on Wednesday.  Delhi LG VK Saxena on Tuesday distributed letters of enrolment to 1669 home guards out of 10,000, for which the recruitment process was started in January, said the statement from the Raj Niwas.  Addressing the newly recruited home guards at an event, the LG said that in the near future additional 15,000 home guards will be added, taking their total strength to over 25,000 it said.  The newly recruited home guards included 226 former civil defence volunteers (CDVs) who were working as bus marshals when they were removed in November last year. The new recruits also included 181 women, the statement said.  The LG in January this year cleared enrolment of 10,285 home guards and directed that the CDVs be given preference in the form of extra credit points in the selection process. However, some candidates approached the court, and as a result, the appointment on 7,939 posts of home guards was kept pending as the matter became sub-judice. The LG, had however, directed appointment of 2,346 home guards who qualified physical measurement and efficiency, and written tests. Out of 2,346 posts, 1669 cleared the medical test and were handed over their appointment letters. In response to the advertisement for 10,285 vacancies, total 1.09 lakh applications were received but only 32,511 reported for the physical test. Meanwhile, the some applicants moved the high court over various issues and a status quo was ordered by the court. The LG has also directed the director general (home guards) to ensure that the remaining 7,939 vacancies are also filled up at the earliest after taking cognizance of the court matters, added the statement.
